title: The transfiguration part 3
scripture_text: ‘’From then on Jesus began to tell his disciples plainly that it was necessary for him to go to Jerusalem, and that he would suffer many terrible things at the hands of the elders, the leading priests, and the teachers of religious law. He would be killed, but on the third day he would be raised from the dead. But Peter took him aside and began to reprimand him for saying such things. “Heaven forbid, Lord,” he said. “This will never happen to you!” Jesus turned to Peter and said, ‘’Get away from me, Satan! You are a dangerous trap to me. You are seeing things merely from a human point of view, not from God’s. Then Jesus said to his disciples, “If any of you wants to be my follower, you must give up your own way, take up your cross, and follow me. If you try to hang on to your life, you will lose it. But if you give up your life for my sake, you will save it. And what do you benefit if you gain the whole world but lose your own soul? Is anything worth more than your soul? or the Son of Man will come with his angels in the glory of his Father and will judge all people according to their deeds. And I tell you the truth, some standing here right now will not die before they see the Son of Man coming in his Kingdom.”
devotional:
Six days later Jesus took Peter and the two brothers, James and John, and led them up a high mountain to be alone. As the men watched, Jesus’ appearance was transformed so that his face shone like the sun, and his clothes became as white as light. Suddenly, Moses and Elijah appeared and began talking with Jesus. Peter exclaimed, “Lord, it’s wonderful for us to be here! If you want, I’ll make three shelters as memorials—one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.” But even as he spoke, a bright cloud overshadowed them, and a voice from the cloud said, “This is my dearly loved Son, who brings me great joy. Listen to him.”The disciples were terrified and fell face down on the ground. Then Jesus came over and touched them. “Get up,” he said.“Don’t be afraid.” And when they looked up, Moses and Elijah were gone, and they saw only Jesus.’ As they went back down the mountain, Jesus commanded them, “Don’t tell anyone what you have seen until the Son of Man has been raised from the dead.” Then his disciples asked him, “Why do the teachers of religious law insist that Elijah must return before the Messiah comes?”Jesus replied, “Elijah is indeed coming first to get everything ready. But I tell you, Elijah has already come, but he wasn’t recognized, and they chose to abuse him. And in the same way they will also make the Son of Man suffer.” Then the disciples realized he was talking about John the Baptist.’’

We need to realise that suffering and glory are often the same thing. In our world view we often compartmentalise life, we have everything boxed up in neat compartments, especially when it comes to suffering and glory. Luke tells us that Moses and Elijah were speaking to Jesus about his death Luke 9:30. They were not talking about his victory, or his splendour, or his majesty, but his death. There are a number of verses in John 13 that clearly show the relationship between glory and suffering.

30. ‘As soon as Judas had taken the bread, he went out. And it was night. 31 When he was gone, Jesus said, “Now the Son of Man is glorified and God is glorified in him. 32 If God is glorified in him, God will glorify the Son in himself, and will glorify him at once.’

Jesus was able to discern the hand and purpose of his father in his suffering. Jesus understood that his suffering was not a random series of undetermined events that were unrelated to the purposes and plans of God. He knew that his suffering had a built-in capacity to bring his Father glory as he went through it.

We need to leave the past behind by learning from it.

Moses and Elijah appeared and began to talk to Jesus. Moses and Elijah were pinnacles of the Jewish faith and spirituality. Moses and Elijah were representatives of the law and the prophets. Moses and Elijah, who were taught to every good Jew, teaching them how to live and please God. But now it was time to listen to a new voice. Moses and Elijah appeared on the mountain before the glory of Jesus to affirm that His voice, His suffering, His Glory is the way. Moses and Elijah had fulfilled their purposes, now it was time to listen to Jesus.

In Jewish liturgy there was a daily prayer called the ‘Shema.’ It is the Hebrew word that begins the most important prayer in Judaism. It is found in Deuteronomy 6:4, which begins with the command to “Hear.” The word ‘Shema’ means to hear. The whole Shema prayer, which includes verses 4-9, of Deuteronomy 6 is spoken daily in the Jewish tradition: look at what Matthew says:

‘’Peter said to Jesus, “Lord, it is good for us to be here. If you wish, I will put up three shelters—one for you, one for Moses and one for Elijah.”While he was still speaking, a bright cloud covered them, and a voice from the cloud said, “This is my Son, whom I love; with him I am well pleased. Listen to him!’’

A voice from heaven, the voice of God speaking directly to the three disciples telling them to listen to his Son. Sometimes we are unable to hear what Jesus is saying to us in the present because we are so accustomed to listening to the voices of the past. We suffer from nostalgic hearing. Although the voices of the past may have been good and important, it is time for a new listening, a new Shema. A new attentiveness to Jesus.

I find it remarkable that as the disciples came down the mountain with Jesus they got into a theological discussion about Elijah. God had just spoken to them from heaven, this is only the second time this had happened in hundreds of years. In the minds of these disciples, Jesus had to be at least equal to Moses an Elijah, but they had not really grasped his full identity. So the Father says ‘This is my Son whom I love, with him I am well pleased, listen to him.’ Here was God the father revealing his heart, talking about what was most important to him, sharing the pleasure he found in Jesus.

As Christians there can be times of uncertainty in our relationship with Jesus. Sometimes we have expectations that are not met, dreams that are dashed and hopes that feel shattered. The Jesus we thought we knew can be different to the Jesus we are experiencing. It is a times like this we need to experience a new intimacy, a new appreciation of his glory, a new realisation that the Jesus we love and worship is greater and bigger than we will ever know or understand.
prayer: Father help me listen to Jesus, more than the legitimate voices of the past.
